title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E740 seeks space curves that extremize an integral of the form ∫ w(v) ds, where v is the distance from a fixed point O and w is a given function of v. Earlier sections showed that the extremal must lie in a plane through O. That plane is z = my + nx, and α, β, γ, δ are the constants of the change to plane coordinates. In that plane Euler uses polar-type coordinates (v, φ), with x = δ v cos φ and αy + βx = δ v sin φ. The tangent direction has angle ψ, with tan ψ = αp + β. The 'principal equation' (from the Euler–Lagrange equations) is (w'v/w) dφ + dψ = 0.

On the previous page Euler set t = v dφ/dv, the tangent of the angle between the radius vector and the tangent line. This gives ψ = φ + arctan t, so the principal equation becomes (w'v/w) dφ + dφ + dt/(1+t²) = 0.

On this page (§40) he removes dφ by writing dφ = t dv/v. Dividing by t gives the separable equation dw/w + dv/v + dt/(t(1+t²)) = 0. Since ∫dt/(t(1+t²)) = ln(t/√(1+t²)), the first integral is w v t/√(1+t²) = C. Because t/√(1+t²) = sin θ, where θ is the angle between radius and tangent, this reads w(v)·v·sin θ = C. In modern terms it is a Clairaut/Bouguer-type invariant: n r sin i = const for rays in a radially stratified medium, or angular momentum in Maupertuis' form of central-force motion. It is the conserved quantity that Noether's theorem attaches to rotational symmetry.

§41 solves for t: t = C/√(w²v² − C²). Hence dφ = C dv/(v√(w²v² − C²)), so φ is given by a quadrature in v, the classical orbit/ray integral. The constants are counted as C, m, n and the new additive constant in φ: four, matching two second-order Euler–Lagrange equations. On the next page Euler recovers x, y, z from v and φ.
errors: No mathematical errors. The integration, the solution for t and the constant count all check.

Euler slightly overstates the novelty of the reduction: once planarity is known, the problem is the planar ∫w(v)ds problem he had already solved in the 1744 Methodus. He himself admits this on the next page.

deep.surprise_reason: A clean but standard derivation of the rotational first integral and the orbit quadrature, already present in Euler's 1744 Methodus and in the refraction literature. The only point of interest is the elegant separation via t, which is a didactic device, not a new result.
transcription_corrections: Transcription of this page is essentially accurate.
